data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The nocturnal UHI emerges from the moisture-memory of the urban surface: impervious surfaces rapidly shed water after rainfall, eliminating latent heat storage; the cross-city gap scales inversely with irrigation and green space, with the largest gaps in dry cities where rural evapotranspiration still occurs but urban evapotranspiration is minimal.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If nocturnal evapotranspiration is negligible in both city and countryside due to stomatal closure at night, the latent heat mechanism is not the primary driver.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If heavily irrigated cities still show large nocturnal UHI due to thermal mass, vegetation is not the controlling variable.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the cross-city gap is better explained by sky view factor than by green space fraction, the moisture-memory mechanism is secondary.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The latent heat flux is a powerful daytime cooling mechanism that carries energy away as water evaporates. Urban impervious surfaces prevent infiltration and storage of moisture, so after sunset there is no latent heat reservoir to draw from and no nighttime evapotranspiration. The countryside, with soil moisture and vegetation, continues to exchange latent heat. The cross-city gap depends on the amount of urban green space and irrigation: cities with less vegetation and irrigation have a larger nocturnal UHI because the urban-rural contrast in latent heat flux is greater and the urban thermal mass retains more sensible heat.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
